Guided Inquiry

1. Predict — which one wins?

Two identical 1 kg masses will be released together from the same displacement. One hangs on two springs joined end to end (series); the other on two springs mounted side by side (parallel). Which one oscillates faster — reaches its equilibrium and returns first?

2. Watch the race

Press ▶ Play. Both masses were pulled 0.10 m below their own equilibrium and released together. Which one gets back to the top first?

The parallel mass — about two of its cycles for every one of the series mass at these settings. Stiffer combination → larger restoring force per metre → larger ω = √(k/m) → shorter period T = 2π√(m/k).

3. Read off the numbers

With k₁ = 100 and k₂ = 200 N/m, is ks larger or smaller than the softer spring, 100 N/m? Then drag k₂ to 400 N/m.

ks = 66.7 N/m — smaller than either spring. Raising k₂ to 400 lifts kp from 300 to 500 N/m but ks only from 66.7 to 80. Since 1/ks = 1/k₁ + 1/k₂ exceeds 1/k₁, ks can never beat the softer spring: in series the soft one sets the limit.

4. The one thing to remember

For springs, series is softer, parallel is stiffer — the opposite of the resistor rule. The two series extensions add, so the same force stretches the pair further; that is what "softer" means. Slide k₁ and k₂ anywhere — can any pair let the series mass win?

No pair can. ks = k₁k₂/(k₁+k₂) sits below both springs, kp = k₁+k₂ above both, so ks < kp always — and T = 2π√(m/k) makes Ts > Tp every time.

The Physics

Two Springs, One Mass — Series vs Parallel · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

The same two springs can hold a mass in two ways: joined end to end, or mounted side by side. The sim hangs a 1 kg mass on each arrangement and releases both together, so you can compare them.

What you'll learn

  • How two spring constants k₁ and k₂ combine into one effective constant k.
  • Why that combined constant depends on how the springs are joined.
  • How the effective constant sets the period T of the hanging mass.
The same two springs, k₁ and k₂, joined two ways. In the second arrangement a rigid bar ties both spring ends to the mass.

What's on screen

  • Left, end to end: two springs in a column with a dot where they join. Arrows x₁ and x₂ give each spring's extension.
  • Right, side by side: two springs and a bar. One arrow x gives the extension of both.
  • Dashed lines mark each mass's equilibrium height.
  • Effective constants panel: the combined k and the period T for each arrangement.
See itHold both masses at the release point. Watch for: a blue column of two springs on the left, and two pink springs with a bar on the right.

03

Springs side by side share one extension

On the right, the bar ties both spring ends to the mass, so both springs always stretch by the same amount x. Each pulls with its own force, k₁x and k₂x, and the two forces add:

F = k₁x + k₂x = (k₁ + k₂) x
Same x, forces add.

The pair acts like one spring of constant

kp = k₁ + k₂

With k₁ = 100 and k₂ = 200 N/m, kp = 300 N/m, more than either spring alone. That is why the sim draws a single extension arrow for the pair.

See itHold the masses at the release point and read the right side. Watch for: one label x = 0.133 m for both springs, and kp = 300.00 N/m in the panel.
04

Springs end to end share one force

On the left, the springs hang one below the other, so the same tension F runs through both. Each stretches by its own amount, x₁ = F/k₁ and x₂ = F/k₂, and the extensions add:

x = x₁ + x₂ = F (1/k₁ + 1/k₂)
Same F, extensions add.

Writing x = F/ks for the pair gives

1/ks = 1/k₁ + 1/k₂, so ks = k₁k₂ / (k₁ + k₂)

With 100 and 200 N/m, ks = 66.7 N/m. The softer spring stretches more: since F is shared, x₁/x₂ = k₂/k₁ = 2.

See itHold the masses at the release point and read the left side. Watch for: x₁ = 0.165 m on the top spring and x₂ = 0.082 m on the bottom one, and ks = 66.67 N/m.
05

End to end is softer than either spring

Since 1/ks = 1/k₁ + 1/k₂ is larger than 1/k₁, ks is smaller than k₁. The same argument gives ks < k₂. The pair is always softer than its softer spring. Likewise k₁ + k₂ is larger than either spring alone.

Making one spring much stiffer does little for the series pair, because the soft spring still stretches. Take k₁ = 100 N/m:

k₂ks (end to end)kp (side by side)
200 N/m66.7 N/m300 N/m
400 N/m80 N/m500 N/m

Equal springs give ks = k/2 and kp = 2k, so kp = 4ks. For any other pair, kp/ks = (k₁ + k₂)²/(k₁k₂) is larger than 4.

See itRaise k₂ from 200 to 400 N/m. Watch for: the panel moving to ks = 80.00 and kp = 500.00 N/m, a small rise for one and a large rise for the other.
06

The stiffer arrangement has the shorter period

Each arrangement acts as one spring of constant k holding the 1 kg mass, so

ω = √(k/m), T = 2π√(m/k)
Larger k, larger ω, shorter T.

With the opening values, Ts = 2π√(1/66.7) = 0.770 s and Tp = 2π√(1/300) = 0.363 s. The ratio is Ts/Tp = √(kp/ks) = 2.12. So the side-by-side mass completes about two cycles for each one on the left. Because kp is at least 4ks, the ratio is never below 2.

Both masses start 0.10 m below equilibrium, so the release is the same. Gravity only moves each equilibrium line down by mg/k. That is 0.147 m on the left and 0.033 m on the right, and the period is unchanged.

See itPress Play with the opening values. Watch for: the pink mass on the right completing about two cycles for each cycle of the blue one.
07

Where it matters

  • Cutting a spring. Cut a uniform spring of constant k into two equal halves and each has 2k, because a shorter piece stretches less for the same force. Joined end to end again, 2k and 2k give ks = (2k)(2k)/(4k) = k, as the rule says.
  • Engine valve springs. Many engines fit two coil springs, one inside the other, on each valve. They compress together, so their constants add, and the pair is stiffer than either.
  • Circuits. Springs follow the capacitor rule: parallel adds, series adds reciprocals. Resistors do the opposite, which is why the resistor rule gives the wrong answer for springs.
08

Summary

In one line. Two springs act as one spring of an effective constant k, found from k₁ and k₂ by a rule that depends on how they are joined, and k then sets the period through T = 2π√(m/k).

Key points

  • Side by side: same extension, forces add, kp = k₁ + k₂.
  • End to end: same force, extensions add, 1/ks = 1/k₁ + 1/k₂.
  • ks is below both springs and kp is above both, so Ts is always longer than Tp.

Common mix-ups

  • "Springs in series add, as resistors do." In series the extensions add, so the pair is softer. It is the side-by-side pair that adds constants.
  • "A bigger k₂ makes the end-to-end pair as stiff as k₂." The soft spring still stretches by x₁ = F/k₁. So ks stays below k₁ however stiff k₂ is.
  • "Gravity changes the period of a hanging mass." It only moves the equilibrium down by mg/k. T = 2π√(m/k) has no g in it.

Things to try on your own

  • Set k₁ = k₂ at three different values and compare kp with ks each time.
  • Set k₁ = 20 N/m and raise k₂ from 20 to 400 N/m. Note how far ks rises and what it stays below.
  • Find the slider pair that makes Ts and Tp differ the most.
